title: Functions, keywords, closures and argument sharing
outcome: Write reusable functions with explicit contracts and distinguish local rebinding from mutation of a passed object.
key_terms: A named argument declared after a semicolon, such as `tol = 1e-8`, that callers pass by name and that does not take part in dispatch.
A function that captures variables from the scope where it is defined and can read them after that scope ends.
A function such as `map`, `filter` or `reduce` that accepts another function as an argument.
A function receives the caller's object itself, so mutating an array argument changes what the caller sees.
A trailing `!` in a name such as `sort!` warns that the function mutates one or more of its arguments.
approach: Read each function's contract from its signature. `affine` uses keywords `scale = 1` and `shift = 0`, `make_scaler` returns a closure over `scale`, `rebind` assigns a new array to its local name, and `change_first!` mutates the caller's array after rejecting empty input. Compare contents with `==` and identity with `===`.

exercises.title: Use defaults
exercises.answer: A default is part of the function contract and should be recorded when it matters scientifically.
exercises.wrong: Assuming unspecified keywords become zero predicts `0 * 5 + 0 = 0`; the defaults in the signature decide.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `affine(5) == 5`; compare it with `affine(5; scale = 0)`, which is 0.

exercises.title: Override one choice
exercises.answer: Explicit keyword configuration makes a transformation reproducible.
exercises.wrong: Passing -2 positionally, as `affine(5, -2)`, raises `MethodError` because `affine` has one positional argument.
exercises.verify: Assert `affine(5; shift = -2) == 3` as the reference does, then confirm the positional call fails.

exercises.title: Build a closure
exercises.task: Create a scale 3 function and apply it to 2.
exercises.hint: The returned function retains its scale binding.
exercises.answer: A closure packages a transformation and context; it does not necessarily copy mutable captured objects.
exercises.why: `make_scaler(3)` returns `x -> 3 * x`, which remembers `scale = 3`, so applying it to 2 gives 6.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the closure to read a global named `scale` at call time would make its result depend on unrelated script state.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `make_scaler(3)(2) == 6`; also map it over `[1, 2]` and expect `[3, 6]`.

exercises.title: Trace a rebound argument
exercises.task: Call rebind on a caller array.
exercises.hint: The local name is assigned another array.
exercises.answer: Rebinding the argument name is different from mutating the shared object.
exercises.why: In `rebind`, `values = [99]` points the local name at a new array, so the caller's `[1]` is untouched.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the caller to see `[99]` assumes assignment writes through the argument, which only element mutation such as `values[1] = 99` does.

exercises.title: Trace a mutated argument
exercises.task: Call change_first! on a nonempty vector.
exercises.expected: Its first element becomes 99 and the returned object aliases it.
exercises.hint: Compare identity as well as contents.
exercises.answer: The naming convention warns callers that the operation changes shared state.
exercises.why: `change_first!` writes `values[1] = 99` into the caller's array and returns that same object.
exercises.wrong: Testing only `returned == [99, 2]` cannot tell a mutated original from a modified copy; identity needs `===`.
exercises.verify: As in worked example B, assert both `values == [99, 2]` and `returned === values`.

exercises.title: Reject an empty mutation
exercises.task: Call change_first! on an empty vector.
exercises.answer: A clear input contract produces a more useful diagnostic than an accidental indexing failure.
exercises.why: The guard `isempty(values) && throw(ArgumentError(...))` runs before indexing, so an empty input gets a named precondition error.
exercises.wrong: Dropping the guard lets `values[1] = 99` raise `BoundsError`, which describes an index rather than the violated contract.
exercises.verify: Assert `@test_throws ArgumentError change_first!(Int[])` as the reference does.

checks_note: The keyword default leaves `affine(5)` unchanged while `shift = -2` moves it to 3, and `make_scaler(3)(2) == 6` shows the closure remembering its factor after the outer call returns. The last group is the important one: `rebind` assigns a new vector to its local name, so the caller's `original` stays `[1]` while the returned `replacement` holds 99 and is a different object. Mutation through `change_first!` is the only way to change the caller's array, and it refuses an empty one.
